en: Chapter One: On Designations (Saṃjñāprakaraṇam) Having prostrated before the illustrious Vāsudeva, the bestower of boons, the illustrious Gaṇeśa, and the Goddess of Speech, I shall expound the Śikṣā— the limb that is the cause of [understanding] the Vedas, which provides excellent clarity and is adorned with the head of its defining characteristics.
Now, I shall explain the designations such as vowels and so forth, for that indeed is their purpose; and I shall declare their results so that the wise may rejoice.

When a sibilant (*ūṣman*) follows, it is above the subsequent part; furthermore, in the case of a contact consonant (*sparśa*), they are indeed the *yamas*.

Thus ends Chapter 22 on the *Aṅgasaṃhitā*. Chapter 23 on *Svarabhakti*: When a spirant (*ūṣman*) follows a vowel, both *repha* (the sound *r*) and *la* constitute a *svarabhakti* [vowel-fragment]. 381.
In the midst of that, one should apply the *svarabhakti* (vowel-fragment) according to the nature of the season (*ṛtu*).
When followed by a consonant (*hapara*), it should end in a consonant (*halanta*) and be closed (*saṃvṛta*);
when following a vowel (*ajanta*) or after the letters *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*, it is declared to be open (*vivṛta*).
The *svarabhakti* (vowel-fragment) following *kareṇū* is *ro*; following *hor*, it becomes *la*, which is called *karviṇī*.
Following *hariṇī*, the *śa* and *ṣa* become *ro*, and the *lakāra* is called *hāritā*.
A *svarabhakti* arises separately from a long vowel (*dīrgha*) and from a non-final vowel (*svāra*). 385–387.
And each [vowel] has its own share of *svarabhakti*; there is no devotion (*bhakti*) in the case of *ha* and *kha*.
(388) Thus ends the section on *svarabhakti*, the twenty-third;
now begins the section on place of articulation (*sthāna*), organ of production (*karaṇa*), and effort (*prayatna*), the twenty-fourth.
As the breath moves within the chest, the *mandra* tone arises;
it is known as *madhyama* when in the throat, and as *tāra* when in the head, according to its own power.
By means of these three, the recitation is uttered in sequence for as long as the study continues. (389–391)
The *nāda* (sound) is the breath (*śvāsa*), while the letter *ha* and the sun (*arka*) are in the throat when it is slightly opened or widely opened.

From the *nāda* arise the unvoiced (*aghoṣa*) letters; the fourth letters of the classes are born from *ha*, while the first letters are born from the breath. The others [the second and third] are from the sun, and from that [the sun] arise the unvoiced *yamas*.
The throat, the middle and end of the mouth and so forth, the roots of the teeth, and the nose;
the palate, the lips, and the chest are the places (*sthāna*) of the phonemes, while those below are the articulators (*karaṇa*).
For the vowel *u*, the two lips are the place; when followed by *au*, they are long.
The throat (kaṇṭha) is said to be at the beginning of the consonants and vowels;
for each letter, there is the distinction between the lips and the palate, whether they are separate or joined.
In the case of *au*, both lips are present; in *o*, they are slightly more or less [open]; thus it is "lips-and-palate" (*oṣṭhatālu*). 398–400.
In the *ka*-group and others, one should touch [the palate] with the middle and ends of the tongue, and with the upper lip; 401.

In the *ṭa*-group, one should touch the middle of the mouth with the tip of the tongue above; 402. And for those [sounds] in the palate produced by the middle and ends [of the tongue], one should touch the tip and middle of the tongue to the *repha* (the letter *r*). 403.
The letter *la* is produced by touching the roots of the teeth with the tip of the tongue from above; the *ūṣman* sounds are produced by the contact of the lips with the teeth;
and the letters *ha* and *visarga* are said to have the throat as their place of articulation.
The effort for the sibilants (*ūṣman*) is dispersed; for the other vowels, it is [concentrated].
(407) For all the simple vowels, a slight degree of contact (*atyalpa-spṛṣṭatā*) is traditionally taught.
(408) Contact (*spṛṣṭatva*) belongs to those known as the stops (*sparśa*); for the others, something slightly more [is said]. (409)

In the second and fourth [classes], it is over-articulated (*atispṛṣṭa*), and in those same places it is equal to them (unaspirated). There, the letter *ha* and the nasal (*nāsikya*) that follows the last [consonant] of each class are known by the wise to be chest-sounds (*urasya*). 410–412.
The *nitya-nāsikya* (permanent nasal), the *yamas*, the *anusvāra*, and the fifth [consonants] are to be known as [nasal].
The vowels (*ajanta*), the semi-vowels (*antastha*), and the letter *ha* are proclaimed to be [nasal] by virtue of their cause.
Thus ends the section on places of articulation, organs of production, and efforts. 24.1–2.
Chapter on the Protracted Vowel (Pluta), 25: If a protracted vowel ending in 'a' is said to be nasalized, it is equal in sound to the *amatra* [vessel] and is designated as *raṅga*. 415–416.
In the *Śloka*, *Gala*, and *Mama* [sections], the vowels *ya*, *ghra*, and *eva* are protracted (*pluta*).
In the *Devā*, *u*, *tām*, *imam*, *ṛvām*, *a*, *svām*, and *aham* [sections], they are long (*dīrgha*) according to the Kaṭha school.
If there are *patnīvats*, they are to be piled; beginning from the *cityas*, those [bricks] are indeed to be performed. 417–419.
The *hotavya* verses, the *satyarāja* sections, those to be emitted (*sṛjyā*), and those to be consumed (*prāśyā*) should be measured;
the *sahasrāmadrā* *soma* offerings and the *krāma* chants should be performed, [reciting] "hā" and "iti.
You, O Brahman, should stand firm over these two-footed beings like Agni; thus [are] the *agā* verses. 420–422.
*hāvaratnīśchinattī ca juhavānī ca gacchatī* (423),
*etī lājīñchācīn*— all these [words] are pluta vowels with the acute accent on the final syllable (424).
*patyā iti*, *gṛhā i tvī*, *uttānā ityaverapāḥ* (425).
Both the Soma-drinkers and the non-Soma-drinkers have attained [the goal]; he has caused them both to stand firm.
(426) He does not know the two Savitra offerings; he does not know the two Agnihotra offerings.
(427) He knows the two Avabhrtha rites; he knows the two animals for the Rbhus and the cooked oblation. (428)
The fire was to be maintained; indeed, there were two, for they find [the goal] as if in a hidden place. 429.
Forty-three syllables above, the ten [syllables] of the four [sections] are prolated (pluta). 430.
From the nineteenth [position], *la* follows *jha*, and there are also the anusvāras born from the visarga. 431.
Including the four *bhakti-yamas*, the castes (*varṇas*) are said to be sixty-six.
(432) Thus ends Chapter 25 on *Pluta*.
Chapter 26 on Labials (*oṣṭhya*).

When the letter *va* is in the middle, when there is an *anusvāra*, in a pause (*virāma*), or when it stands in conjunction (*saṃyuta*), and even when followed by the vowel *au* in its manifest form (*vyakti*), both [lips] are determined to be doubled. Furthermore,
when *ha* is in the middle of a conjunction of labials, and when *pa* follows a *visarga*, [the same applies].
Having filled [the mouth] with air through the two palates, it is known as the *māṇḍūka* [breath], which is superior.

(436) When two consonants (*sparśa*) meet, whether in the recitation or at a pause, a slight sound of the first [consonant] should be understood, as indeed there is [a sound] of the letter *m* at the pause. (437–438)
At the pause (*virāma*), a separate effort (*prayatna*) is made for a consonant preceded by another of its own class.
However, in the case of *oṃ*, the labial group (*pavarga*), and when [a consonant] follows [a vowel], there is no such separate effort.
Thus ends section 26 on the Labials (*oṣṭhya*).
Chapter 27: Determination of Time.
One should know the characteristics of time as follows: that which is uttered by a blue jay consists of one mātrā; by a crow, it is two mātrās; and by a peacock, it is three mātrās. (441–442)
Time that is extremely subtle is an atom (aṇu); half a mātrā is a manifest mātrā.
The duration of time it takes to snap one's fingers is a mātrā. That which is preceded by a consonant and followed by a consonant is proclaimed as an atom-mātrā (aṇumātra).
In a pause (*virāma*), between two phonemes (*varṇa*), there is a duration of two *mātrās* even when they are not joined.
A *hal* (consonant) has devotion [to the following vowel]; *visarga* is at the end; after a short vowel, *ṇ* and *y* follow.
Above a *sparśa* (stop), *v* is half a *mātrā*; these [consonants] are at the end; *l* has three-quarters [of a *mātrā*].

At the end of a visarga, there shall be a half-mora pause; likewise when followed by *kṣa* or *pa*. When combined with a following consonant, and in the case of labials (*oṣṭhya*) such as *au* and *ai*, the pause occurs before the preceding [vowel]. In the case of long and equal vowels, it is like an ant; when there is homogeneity (*savarṇatā*), it is like a cooking process within a single word.
The following of a vowel after a *visarga* is observed even when there is no similarity [of pitch]; however, the durations for the pause (*virāma*) are primarily those of the short vowels.
(452) In the *Svarodaya*, the *anusvāra* shall have a duration of half a short vowel;
the pause (*virāma*) occurs between those two, specifically for the long and protracted vowels. (453–454)
At the end of the *praṇava*, after the letters of the *pavarga* class, and at the very end of an *avagraha*,
as well as at the end of a sentence, a pause (*virāma*) of one and a half *mātrās* is prescribed. However, between a word and a *praṇava*, the pause shall always consist of two *mātrās*.

When there is a connection with its own vowel, the duration of those two [anusvāra and repha] is like that of their respective vowels. (458) Anusvāra has a duration of two mātrās when followed by *repha* or a sibilant (*ūṣman*). (459) When followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyukta*), this [anusvāra] is proclaimed to have a duration of one mātrā. (460)

After a short vowel, the *ṅa* and *na* [nasals] occurring above a *kha* or above a *kha* become two-mora (long) sounds; likewise, when followed by a *ṣa*, they are always [long] above a *kha*. Similarly, when followed by a *ha* that is itself followed by a consonant (*hal*), and also when not joined with another [consonant], the *na* becomes one-mora after a long vowel, provided there is a *ya* or *va* following it. 461–463.
A short vowel-syllable (nāda) should consist of two mātrās; elsewhere, it may also be of one mātrā.
However, in the case of the *praṇava* alone, the vowel should be one and a half mātrās.
In the *Yajus*, that which ends in the letter *m* is high-pitched (*udātta*), while the six beginning with *om* are circumflex (*svarita*).

One [syllable] with one, two, or three morae; three [syllables] as one, and two as one; two [syllables] as two; 467. The state of having three morae belongs to the pause at the end of a *ṛc* and also at the end of a half-verse; 468.
"Let the Hotṛ worship" (*hotā yakṣat*) occurs at the end, and "the divine *barhis*" (*devaṃ barhiḥ*) in the fifth [case]. 469.

In the *Sahāmbhasi*, the question regarding the ancestors (*pitṛpraśna*) would be an *ṛc* if it is accompanied by the *nidhana*; at the end of a section (*kāṇḍa*), a question, or an *anuvāka*, there are ten, eight, or five morae (*mātrā*). However, when the texts are complete, the time is said to be tripled.

A vowel with one measure (mātrā) is short, while that with two measures is long; a vowel with three measures is protracted (pluta). Indeed, a quarter of a vowel is a fourth measure. There are three modes of speech for a sentence: rapid, slow, and medium. 473–475.
And when there is a difference in time regarding their occurrence, then there would be a difference in the action;
for it is said that those phonemes arise from effort and from time.
Since they would be absent in the absence of those two, both [effort and time] should be correctly understood as such. 476–478.
Thus, by resorting to the middle course, the times have been well-determined. Indeed, in the Prātiśākhyas and other such works, this very same course has been adopted.
Thus ends the section on the determination of time. 27.
Chapter 28: On the Fruit of Recitation. There is no pause at a single word; one should utter [the mantra] very clearly.
Not after *na*, *hi*, *u*, *vā*, *sma*, *ha*, *tu*, *īm*, *vai*, *nu*, *ete* (these particles), nor below a *kūṭa* (a conjunct consonant). 481–482.
Or rather, the vowels *śrī*, *de*, *gha*, and *dhayā* should be established as long when they have reached their own [natural] state.

(483) It is not so for those connected with the third [syllable], even in another application. (484) A syllable followed by a consonant and ending in a vowel is long; other than that, it is light. (485)
In this regard, the wise have recorded that there are three groups of three syllables each:

*tri*, *lo*, *na*; *svo*, *stri*, *gur*; and *mo*, *bhūḥ*, *ādi*. Among these, *ka* and *ndra* are auspicious at the beginning; *u*, *ya*, and *bha* are auspicious at the end; *so* and *'ni* cause distress in the middle; and *ra* and *ja* correspond respectively to fire and the sun.
The letters *da*, *dha*, *ta*, *tha*, *pa*, *pha*, *na*, and *ma* are the first [consonants] of each class; those followed by *kṣa* are nasalized (*nāsikya*). 489.
Wind, fire, earth, moon, and sun are the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) of the five [classes]. 490.
The Brahmin caste is high (*ucca*), while the Kṣatriya caste is low (*nīcaka*). 491.
The *vaiśya* caste is the *svāra*, while the *śūdra* is known as the *pracaya*. The *udātta* is declared to be *sāttvika*, and the *svarita* is known as *rājasa*.
The wise know these two, the *nihata* and the *pracaya*, to be *tāmasa*.
The vowels and the first [class of consonants] are the Brahmin castes;
the second [class] are said to be the Kṣatriya castes;
and the semivowels (*mantasthā*) are indeed proclaimed as the Vaiśyas. 495–497.

The *anusvāra* and the *visarga* are indeed remembered as the youngest of the *ūṣman* sounds. (498) Whatever other class [of sound] is mentioned, that shall be their means of withdrawal (*saṃhāraka*).
(499) In the utterance of those [sounds], the preservation of their respective classes occurs. (500)

In the utterance of the phonemes (*varṇa*), the complete definition is traditionally recorded: (501) the absence of deficiency or excess, the state of Brahman, and recitation with devotion. (502) Clarity, a melodious tone, fortitude, and one-pointedness of mind—these are the four qualities. (503)
One who is devoted to this should recite the Veda; he attains the fruit of the Veda (504).
Being vigilant and wise, one should remain at the beginning and end of each chapter (505).
For the protection of the Vedas, one should always utter the syllable *Oṃ* (506).
If it is not recited at the beginning, it flows away; if it is not recited at the end, it falls apart.
Therefore, it should have the *praṇava* at both its beginning and its end, as well as its ancillary parts (*aṅga*).
Furthermore, there are the characteristics of the phonemes (*varṇa*) and the junctions of words (*pada-sandhi*) within the *saṃhitā*.
The wise know that the Chandas and other such treatises are indeed the auxiliary sciences (upāṅgas). 510.

Phoneme (dhvani), place of articulation (sthāna), organ of articulation (karaṇa), effort (prayatna), duration (kālatā), accent (svara), deity (devatā), and genus (jāti)—by these means are letters (varṇas) to be understood by the discerning. 511–512.
The Yajurveda has tawny eyes, a slender waist, and a large neck;
it has broad cheeks, black feet, and is copper-colored. Born of the Kāśyapa lineage, he who recites even a single chapter without the proper characteristics [of the deity] at all times— 513–515.
Indeed, neither that Brahmin nor even that virtuous person attains its fruit [if they do not know this].

(516) The characteristics of the Saṃhitā, of words, and of syllables, as well as of time and so forth; (517) and likewise the characteristics of the euphonic combinations (*saṃdhi*) of *hal* consonants, *visarga*, vowels (*ac*), and accents (*svara*). (518)
He who, having correctly understood these eight characteristics,
recites this second chapter, is said to be the Supreme Brahman; whether reciting the *saṃhitā*, the *pada*, the *krama*, or the *jaṭā* [arrangements of the Veda], he is indeed Brahman.
One who knows the characteristics then attains the eternal knowledge of Brahman (522). He who drinks the nectar of the Vedas becomes, because of that, a true brāhmaṇa (523).
And thus, he who knows the Vyāsa-śikṣā is called a lord among brāhmaṇas (524).

The wise and disciplined person who recites this instruction issued from the throat of the illustrious Vyāsakaṇṭha, whose mind is perfectly full of the glorious Supreme Brahman, indeed attains all his desired objects. (525) Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter on the fruits of recitation.
